Attended AMA webinar: Using AI with judgement

Session covered environmental impacts, developing AI models using the Latent Space Game, practical examples using Theory Machine mechanics, and the 4D AI fluency framework. Also group discussion on when AI-generated imagery should or should not be approved in individual organisations.

General consensus was that fully AI generated images would not be approved, with discussion around accuracy and the impact on illustrators/artists. In terms on editing, some AI image editing could be approved dependent on context, but in most cases non-AI options (e.g. cropping the offending area out of the image manually) would give similar or better effects. All agreed that generating backgrounds which do not exist, or removing key identifying aspects of a venue space were not acceptable and would not be approved.

OCMAT Family Magazine (Edition 4)

As part of my role, I have created and developed the Trust’s Family Magazine, now in its fourth edition, published three times a year. The magazine has become a key communication tool, designed to bring together families, staff and wider community members across our Trust in a clear, accessible and inclusive way.

The purpose of the magazine is to provide a single, cohesive platform where everything we want to share as a Trust can be found in one place. This includes strategic updates, celebration of success, community engagement, staff recruitment, parental support and practical information. By doing this, the magazine supports consistency of messaging across all schools, while still allowing space for each school’s individual identity and achievements to shine.

This fourth edition demonstrates how the magazine has matured into a strategic Trust-wide publication. It opens with From Your Editor and From Your CEO, setting the tone and ensuring families feel directly connected to Trust leadership and decision-making. Sections such as Your Voice, Our Trust reinforce our commitment to listening to parents and carers, encouraging two-way communication rather than one-way information sharing.

The magazine includes comprehensive Trust Updates, alongside features such as Working for Us and Our Lives News, helping families and staff understand not only what is happening, but why it matters. Community-focused content, including Celebrating our PTFAs, Volunteering, and Upcoming Trust-Wide Events, strengthens relationships across schools and reinforces our Trust values of Community, Compassion and Inclusion.

Celebration is a strong theme throughout the magazine. This spreadsheet lays the groundwork for generating meaningful insights that will help us:

To optimise these efforts, the chapter highlights essential metrics. New lead volume, conversion rates, average transaction value, and the break‑even point. Subscription businesses should also track monthly recurring revenue, churn rate, and overall CLV to understand sustained performance.

A key theme is focusing on your “Tribe”, loyal, high‑value customers who advocate for your brand. These customers yield the greatest returns, while low‑value or resource‑heavy customers may be worth letting go. Finally, the chapter reinforces the importance of Net Promoter Score (NPS), a straightforward measure of customer satisfaction based on likelihood to recommend. Scores above +50 indicate strong advocacy and a healthy customer base.

With having a premium position in the building materials market, it is important for ARDEX to upsell the additional benefits the prospect receives if they were to purchase ARDEX products, this includes an on-hand Technical Support Team to answer any queries and provide recommendations on site, a loyalty app that provides lucrative cashback rewards when ARDEX products are purchased and also a 10 year warranty when ARDEX products are used in the correct manner, providing both the installer and customer with piece of mind that they will not receive any callbacks when products fail to perform.

Moving the forward, the business should focus on gathering NPS from our customers, this could be to find out if they would recommend ARDEX to another trade professional based on products, our technical support services or about our GivBax Rewards loyalty programme. Linkedin platform experiment 

I carried out a LinkedIn content experiment for Able Training to explore whether a more concept-led and visually different post could reach people beyond our existing network. Instead of following the format of our usual LinkedIn content, I developed a more creative “receipt-style” concept designed to interrupt the normal feed and encourage people to stop and look at the post. This helped me consider how different creative approaches, hooks and formats can be used to attract attention while still communicating an appropriate marketing message. (K1.1, S1.3)

After publishing the post, I monitored its early performance and compared the results with a previous Able Training LinkedIn post. Within approximately 17 minutes, the experimental post had received 144 impressions. More importantly, around 86% of those impressions came from people outside our existing network. In comparison, a previous post had received 127 impressions with approximately 87% of its audience coming from within our existing network. This showed me that content format can potentially influence how LinkedIn initially distributes a post and helped me understand why reach should be analysed in more detail than simply looking at the overall impression number. (K3.1, S5.1)

I also reviewed the engagement alongside the reach. Although the new post was initially being distributed to a much wider out-of-network audience, it had not yet generated likes or comments at the point of the early review. I considered how LinkedIn may test content with an audience and how continued distribution can depend on the response it receives. This helped me distinguish between reach and meaningful engagement and reinforced the importance of reviewing several KPIs together rather than judging content success from one metric. (S5.1, K1.1)

I compared the experimental post with more traditional content we had previously published and reflected on what could be learned from the difference in distribution. The exercise helped me understand the value of testing different creative approaches rather than repeatedly using the same format. It also showed me that an unusual concept may help content reach new audiences, but the content still needs to generate enough interest and engagement for that reach to translate into stronger overall performance. I will use this learning when planning future social media content by testing different hooks and formats and using performance data to decide what should be developed further. Competitive pricing research 

I have done some research into competitive pricing for the US events. Here is what we offer for our US events:

WORKTECH Events (1-day future of work and workplace)
Customer segments: Senior workplace leaders from HR, CRE, IT, FM, and A+D
USP: Global learning and a strong network of expert speakers
Pricing model: Tiered pricing from Super Early Bird to Early Bird and Standard rate, with some other discounts available
Indicative price: Base price shown is $549, with a standard price of $649

Here are the top 6 competitors in the US, their customer segments, USP, pricing model, prices, and how they compare to WORKTECH events:

1) CoreNet Global – North America Summit (CRE end-users + service partners)
Customer segments: Corporate Real Estate (end-users), workplace leaders, plus major CRE suppliers/service providers.
USP: Flagship CRE association summit; big networking + membership-driven community.
Pricing model: High-price, tiered registration with member vs non-member price visibility.
Indicative price: Base price shown: $2,835 for a 3-day pass.May include other networking/workshop events.
Compared to WORKTECH: Competes for senior CRE time/budget but is a very different spend level (often paid via professional development budgets).

2) IFMA – World Workplace (FM / workplace operations + expo)
Customer segments: Facilities Management leaders, workplace operations, service providers; strong expo draw.
USP: “Premier FM conference + expo” with a large vendor ecosystem and education.
Pricing model: Multi-tiered (presale → tiers) + member vs regular + daily vs full event.
Indicative prices (2026 reg form): Full Event: $800–$1,225 (member), $1,000–$1,425 (regular); Daily $450–$875 (member), $550–$975 (regular). A 3-day event that includes networking events throughout.
Compared to WORKTECH: Still pricier than you, but closer—WORKTECH can position as more boutique/curated (and easier to get approved).

3) SHRM – Annual Conference (HR mega-conference)
Customer segments: HR leaders, People/DEI, talent, generalist HR; huge scale.
USP: Largest HR conference positioning; broad HR education + expo.
Pricing model: Tiered (Preview/Early/Standard/On-site) + member/nonmember.
Indicative prices (SHRM26): $2,095 preview, $2,395 early bird, $2,595 standard, $2,695 on-site (member pricing shown; nonmember higher). A 4-day conference with networking events. 
Compared to WORKTECH: Different category (mega). Your pricing is far more accessible, but SHRM competes for calendar space for HR/People leaders.

4) HR Technology Conference (HRIT buyers + vendors)
Customer segments: HR tech buyers, HR leaders evaluating tools, HRIT teams; heavy vendor/expo.
USP: Large HR tech marketplace + sessions; very vendor-driven.
Pricing model: Conference pass with discount pricing; team bundles.
Indicative prices (Oct 2026): $1,295 (discount) / $1,995 (list) for a conference pass. The ticket includes networking events and social activities. 
Compared to WORKTECH: More “buying software” oriented and expensive; you can win by emphasizing strategic workplace transformation + cross-discipline (CRE/Workplace/Tech/HR).

5) Future of Work USA (Dallas) – HR/EX/Digital Workplace focus
Customer segments: HR/People, EX, Internal Comms, Digital Workplace.
USP: Track-based agenda; strong HR/EX orientation.
Pricing model: Pass tiers (Bronze/Silver/Gold) with early bird pricing.
Indicative prices: $560 (1-day) / $920 (2-day) / $1,600 (gold) early bird for the 3-day event. VIP tickets include access to roundtables and other networking events.
Compared to WORKTECH: This is closest to your “future of work” lane and overlaps with the audience—your advantage is workplace/CRE depth + curated end-user room (if you protect that mix).

6) Bisnow (NYC CRE events as an “alternative spend”)
Customer segments: CRE owners/investors/developers + brokers; some corporate CRE depending on topic.
USP: Local market specificity + frequent events.
Pricing model: Lower-cost tickets, often with tiered pricing as inventory moves.
Indicative price example (NY event): $155 ticket shown (and notes pricing tiers increase) for a 1-day event.
Compared to WORKTECH: Not the same “future of work” format, but competes for CRE attention with cheap, local, frequent options.

Overall, the WORKTECH 1-day event fits in competitively to offer the customers from each audience segment a different product or offer at a competitive price with similar benefits of expo, networking, learning, and discussions. 

WORKTECH is accessible with its competitive price and 1 day committment for busy end-users.
